transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~90 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marco Li (Redwood Infra), Dana Rhee (Redwood Solutions), Elliot Vaughn (Cobalt CTO), Sara Kim (Cobalt ML Platform), Jonas Becker (Cobalt Lead Eng), Priya Nair (Cobalt Security), Tomas Ruiz (Cobalt SRE)

Summary:
High-level technical deep dive to design an architecture for supporting persistent KV cache for ultra-long-context (128k+ tokens) workloads. Focus areas: sparse attention strategies, KV sharding and eviction, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization impact on cache size & perf, and on-prem/VPC integration (KMS/HSM + audit logs).

Topics Covered:
- Persistent KV store options (in-memory vs SSD tiering)
- Sparse / hybrid attention patterns (chunked local attention, global tokens, attention tiling)
- Sequence sharding and KV distribution for multi-GPU inference
- Batching strategies for sub-100ms SLOs vs throughput optimization
- Quantization profiles and mixed-precision inference impact on cache fidelity
- Private deployment constraints: network egress, KMS integration, SOC2 auditability

Action items (quick): see metadata for owners/due dates.

Transcript:
[00:00:12] Alex Monroe: alright everyone, thanks for joining, um today's goal is to walk through what a persistent KV backed long-context architecture looks like for the 128k-plus use case for Cobalt. we'll try to keep it pretty concrete—pri, you on deck to kick off?
[00:00:32] Priya Desai: yeah thanks alex. i'll start with a quick overview of patterns we've seen in other customers. there's basically three levers: how you chunk and index long documents, how you store the KV state (in-memory vs tiered), and how you route requests to shards for low-latency. for 128k we usually combine chunking with sparse attention to avoid quadratic blowup.
[00:01:05] Elliot Vaughn: can you clarify 'sparse attention' — like is it our modification or model-level change? our models are fairly standard transformers, we can't retrain much here.
[00:01:18] Priya Desai: good point. i'm using sparse as an inference-time strategy: we do local sliding-window attention on chunks plus global tokens for document-level context. it's more of a runtime attention scheduling / mask than a model re-architecture. so no retraining needed.
[00:01:38] Sara Kim: so the runtime builds a map of token positions -> chunk ids and then only materializes KV for the active window? how do you handle cross-chunk references?
[00:01:52] Priya Desai: yep. we keep a persistent KV index keyed by chunk id and token-range. for cross-chunk references we maintain a small 'global' KV that captures summary embeddings or anchor tokens—cheap to keep in memory. that's the hybrid approach.
[00:02:12] Jonas Becker: what's the latency hit for reconstructing cross-chunk attention if you need to pull from SSD? our SLO is 200ms tail.
[00:02:24] Marco Li: this is where tiering matters. if your working set fits in GPU memory + host DRAM we can hit 100-200ms for single-token generation with micro-batching. once you cross to NVMe reads for misses it's much higher — 600ms to seconds depending on IO pattern. we bias toward warm caches and prefetching.
[00:02:48] Tomas Ruiz: prefetching sounds risky for large corpora — you can't prefetch everything. how do you predict locality?
[00:02:58] Priya Desai: we use a combination of LShed-style LRU, workload-aware hints (from app), and cheap fingerprinting of prompts to identify hot chunks. also customer-provided session affinities help—if a user tends to browse the same doc, that's easy to warm.
[00:03:16] [interruption: background mic noise]
[00:03:30] Alex Monroe: moving on to sharding—pri, can you walk through our recommended shard topology for 4-8 GPU nodes?
[00:03:37] Priya Desai: sure. two patterns: 1) KV-sharded: each GPU holds KV for a subset of chunk ids and also runs attention for requests routed to it; 2) Model-sharded: model weights are split across GPUs but KV is replicated or served from a dedicated KV tier. KV-sharded is simpler for ultra-long context because KV locality keeps IO low, but it requires smart routing.
[00:04:04] Elliot Vaughn: smart routing meaning a lookup to the directory before every request? that's extra hop.
[00:04:10] Marco Li: we keep the directory compact in redis or ring metadata — the lookup is <1ms if colocated, and we batch them into the request flow so it's amortized. important to avoid cross-GPU network shuffles at token-time.
[00:04:26] Sara Kim: what about consistency when you have updates to KV (e.g., streaming ingestion of new tokens)?
[00:04:33] Priya Desai: we support append-only writes and serve a last-good snapshot for inference. writes are pushed to a write-queue and materialized asynchronously; reads see a consistent snapshot per request. for strict linearizability we can add stronger sync but that's costly. most customers accept eventual materialization for scale.
[00:04:50] Jonas Becker: quantization—how aggressive can we be before cache semantics break? we saw hallucination drift when moving from fp16 to q4_a in our QA tests.
[00:04:59] Priya Desai: yep, quantization interacts with KV fidelity. for KV caching, reduced precision compresses KV size but introduces small numeric drift. recommended approach: keep KV in high-precision on the host (fp16) and quantize the model execution path only. or, use mixed-KV: keep keys in int8 for lookup and values in fp16 for reconstruction. we'll demonstrate tradeoffs in the benchmark.
[00:05:23] [00:05:30] Priya Nair: from security angle, if KV holds PII we need encryption at rest and key rotation via our HSM. how does Redwood integrate?
[00:05:39] Dana Rhee: we integrate with customer KMS/HSM via gRPC encrypted calls; we support envelope encryption for KV blobs and have audit hooks for reads/writes. for private deployment we can run the control plane in the customer's VPC — no egress.
[00:05:55] Priya Nair: audit hooks meaning per-token audit logs? that smells expensive.
[00:06:03] Dana Rhee: it's configurable. you can log chunk-level accesses instead of per-token. we also sample the logs and emit deltas to downstream SIEMs.
[00:06:10] Alex Monroe: okay, let's go through a concrete request flow for a 150k token prompt split into 3MB of chunks—what happens step-by-step?
[00:06:21] Priya Desai: request arrives at edge, route policy picks dedicated pool. router checks directory for chunk ids covering the prompt (this is the metadata lookup). for each chunk we check prefix cache (local GPU DRAM), then host DRAM, then NVMe tier; we assemble active KV for the requested windows, apply attention masks to only materialize local windows + global tokens, then run decoding with prefix cache warm.
[00:06:47] Marco Li: note the assembly step parallelizes across GPUs—prefetch threads can overlap NVMe reads with GPU computation to hide IO. but that requires careful temp buffer sizing to avoid blowing GPU memory.
[00:07:01] Jonas Becker: is batching across users feasible here? our use-case is interactive so batching hurts latency.
[00:07:08] Priya Desai: we support micro-batching (2-8 requests) to keep latency under SLO while improving token throughput. adaptive batching triggers only when it doesn't violate per-request latency budgets.
[00:07:20] Elliot Vaughn: what's the best way to size chunk length? we tried 8k chunks and had too many cross-chunk lookups.
[00:07:29] Priya Desai: chunking is workload dependent. longer chunks reduce cross-chunk references but increase per-chunk KV size and risk of large misses. a heuristic: pick a chunk size that captures semantic paragraphs for your content—8k for code-heavy logs might be too small; 32k or 64k chunks often hit a good tradeoff for docs. we'll run experiments on your corpus.
[00:07:47] [00:08:10] Sara Kim: are there runtime-level attention optimizations we should use? i've heard about sparse attention kernels and tiling.
[00:08:17] Priya Desai: yes, we use attention tiling to compute local windows with fused kernels that reduce memory bandwidth. for global tokens we run a smaller global attention pass. newer GPUs (H100) have sparse compute primitives that we leverage; but you need kernels compiled for the right architecture or fallback to dense.
[00:08:38] Marco Li: also, KV compression helps—store values compressed on NVMe and decompress into host DRAM. compression reduces IO but adds CPU latency; it's a classic tradeoff.
[00:08:50] Tomas Ruiz: curious about failure modes—if a GPU node dies, do we fall back to hosted smaller model or re-route?
[00:08:58] Alex Monroe: we support two fallback policies: warm-fallback to a smaller compatible model (faster to spin up), or auto-route to spare capacity. for strict availability you can opt for geo-redundant replicas for KV metadata.
[00:09:12] Jonas Becker: latency percentiles — can you share observed p95/p99 numbers for 128k workloads?
[00:09:19] Priya Desai: rough ballpark from similar customers: p50 single-token gen ~80-120ms, p95 ~250-500ms, p99 depends on misses and IO — could be 1-3s if NVMe reads are involved. our goal is to keep most of the traffic in the in-memory working set.
[00:09:36] Elliot Vaughn: anything special for multi-tenant security on shared dedicated pools?
[00:09:43] Dana Rhee: RBAC, VPC isolation, per-tenant metrics, and encrypted per-tenant KV namespaces. for extra isolation we recommend dedicated pools per tenant.
[00:09:52] [00:10:20] Alex Monroe: okay, let's pivot to concrete perf testing plan—pri, what tests will give us helpful signals?
[00:10:27] Priya Desai: we'll run three main tests: 1) Warm-cache run: working set pre-warmed to fit in DRAM+GPU to measure ideal latency; 2) Cold-cache run: randomize access to force NVMe misses to measure worst-case; 3) Mixed-run: realistic access pattern from your telemetry to measure tail behavior. for each run we'll measure p50/p95/p99 latency, sustained tokens/sec, and KV hit-rate.
[00:10:51] Sara Kim: can you include quantization variations? we want to compare fp16 vs q4 vs q8 for throughput and any QA/regression impact.
[00:10:59] Priya Desai: yes we'll include quant buckets. we'll also include a micro-eval to detect hallucination/regression on our standard eval set.
[00:11:07] Tomas Ruiz: for on-prem, network egress is a hard no. can Redwood control plane be air-gapped?
[00:11:15] Dana Rhee: we have a Private deployment mode where the control plane runs in your VPC; for fully air-gapped we offer an on-prem package with local control plane and optional physical key exchange for licensing. separate discussion but doable.
[00:11:27] [00:11:45] Elliot Vaughn: cost — rough order of magnitude for a dedicated 4xH100 pool with 2TB NVMe for KV?
[00:11:52] Alex Monroe: we'll send a draft estimate. quick thumb: depends on committed hours and support level; we'll include amortized NVMe and operations in the spreadsheet.
[00:12:05] Priya Desai: technical note—when you're doing KV-sharded model, one must be careful about KV broadcast patterns during generation; broadcasting large KV values across interconnect kills perf. so we keep values local and only send minimal routing information.
[00:12:24] Jonas Becker: what's the best serialization format for KV blobs? protobuf, flatbuffers, custom?
[00:12:30] Marco Li: we use a compact binary encoding with a small schema version to allow rolling upgrades. base design: key (64-bit fingerprint) + metadata + compressed payload. protobuf is fine but adds size; flatbuffers or a custom binary are lower overhead.
[00:12:43] [00:13:10] Priya Nair: regulatory question: can you support per-country data residency for KV shards? we have EU/US split requirements.
[00:13:18] Dana Rhee: yes - shards can be pinned to regions and the routing policy will prefer local shards. for dedicated pools you can provision region-specific capacity and restrict cross-region fallback.
[00:13:30] Alex Monroe: demo time—pri, can you show the perf spreadsheet and an example request trace?
[00:13:37] [screen share: perf-spreadsheet-redwood-cobalt-v1.xlsx]
[00:13:40] Priya Desai: here is the trace for a warm-cache single request: timeline shows directory lookup 0.8ms, local KV assembly 28ms, attention compute 60ms, token emit 12ms. the cold-cache trace has NVMe reads at 240ms.
[00:13:58] Jonas Becker: can you share the spreadsheet link?
[00:14:02] Alex Monroe: shared in chat — https://redwood-internal.example.com/perf/cobalt/128k-v1 (note: placeholder link)
[00:14:10] Sara Kim: on the NVMe front, do you recommend local NVMe per node or a shared NVMe pool?
[00:14:17] Marco Li: local NVMe per node reduces network IO and is better for tail latency. shared NVMe (like networked block store) simplifies operations but adds network latency and variability. for best tail we recommend local NVMe + replication for redundancy.
[00:14:31] Tomas Ruiz: how much host DRAM do you typically need per GPU for a 128k use-case?
[00:14:36] Priya Desai: ballpark: plan for ~1.5x-2x the GPU KV footprint in host DRAM to handle assembly buffers and decompression. exact numbers depend on chunk size and quantization.
[00:14:49] Elliot Vaughn: about 3rd-party libs — are you using Triton or custom kernels?
[00:14:54] Marco Li: both. we use Triton for many kernels but maintain custom fused kernels for attention tiling that give the best perf on H100. we also JIT compile kernels per-model shape when beneficial.
[00:15:07] [00:15:40] Priya Desai: another practical tip—use prefix/KV warming during user session initialization rather than first interactive call. a short background warm request can pre-populate hot chunks into GPU memory. that reduces first-call tail.
[00:15:54] Jonas Becker: regeneration behavior—if we reroll prompt and tokens move, does the KV map change and cause churn?
[00:16:00] Priya Desai: KV map is keyed by chunk id (stable) so regenerations that alter offsets within the same chunk are cheap. only if the chunking boundary changes significantly will you get different KV keys. we also keep anchor summaries to mitigate small shifts.
[00:16:18] Sara Kim: any gotchas for tokenizers? our internal tokenizer has some heuristics that split unevenly and cause off-by-one chunks.
[00:16:25] Priya Desai: tokenizer determinism is important. we recommend canonicalizing tokenization in the pipeline and storing chunk boundaries alongside token offsets so you avoid mismatches between chunk id computed at ingest vs runtime.
[00:16:36] [00:17:05] Alex Monroe: five-minute check — friends on security, does this address your main concerns?
[00:17:10] Priya Nair: yes mostly — will need the SOC2 and dataflow diagrams. please include how audit logs are retained and how keys are rotated.
[00:17:19] Dana Rhee: we'll include the diagrams in the security packet.
[00:17:24] Elliot Vaughn: timeline—if we approve pilot can we have a POC in 3 weeks?
[00:17:30] Alex Monroe: that's feasible. first step is perf test on smaller scale next week then pilot kickoff mid-November.
[00:17:37] [00:18:00] Priya Desai: last technical note — for models with huge KV sizes we sometimes apply bloom filters on the directory to avoid unnecessary NVMe reads for non-existent chunk ids; it's a small memory win that reduces IO.
[00:18:12] Jonas Becker: clever. cost of false positives?
[00:18:15] Priya Desai: tuned low; it's more a quick reject to avoid reads.
[00:18:22] [ambient typing]
[00:18:45] Alex Monroe: wrapping up—recap and immediate next steps: 1) Redwood to run warm/cold/mixed 128k perf tests on H100 sim cluster and share spreadsheet; 2) Cobalt to provide sample corpus and list of hot flows; 3) security packet + VPC/airgap options shared by alex; 4) schedule pilot kickoff week of 2026-11-16.
[00:19:10] Elliot Vaughn: sounds good. one more question — we sometimes need deterministic outputs for audit. does caching affect determinism?
[00:19:18] Priya Desai: caching is deterministic if the model and kv snapshot are consistent. we recommend capturing a snapshot id for each inference so you can replay deterministically.
[00:19:28] Sara Kim: thanks all, looking forward to the perf results.
[00:19:34] Alex Monroe: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email and update the CRM.
